books.title: The Very Hungry Caterpillar
books.author: Eric Carle
books.why: A simple, rhythmic count-through-the-week structure that even very young children can predict and join in with.
talkPrompts: What foods did the caterpillar eat? Can you remember the order?
Why do you think the caterpillar got a stomach ache?
What do you think it feels like inside a cocoon?
Have you ever seen a real caterpillar or butterfly outside?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: let children join in on the repeated "but he was still hungry" line.
Third read: pause before each new food and let children guess what comes next.
books.lookFor: Look at the holes punched through the pages where the caterpillar has eaten — can you find and count them?

books.title: We're Going on a Bear Hunt
books.author: Michael Rosen
books.why: A call-and-response rhythm and repeated refrain that gets a whole group moving and joining in together.
talkPrompts: Which of the places they travel through would you find trickiest, and why?
What do you think the bear is thinking as the family runs home?
Can you remember the order of all the places they go through?
Why do you think they run home so fast at the end?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: let children do the matching action and sound for each obstacle before you turn the page.
Third read: whisper the "uh-oh" moments together for suspense.
books.lookFor: Look at the family's faces on each page — how does their expression change as the journey gets trickier?

books.title: The Gruffalo
books.author: Julia Donaldson
books.why: A clever, rhyming trickster story where a tiny character outwits every bigger animal it meets.
talkPrompts: Why does the mouse keep inventing the gruffalo in the first place?
What do you think each animal is afraid of, and why?
How does the mouse manage to scare off the real gruffalo at the end?
If you invented a scary creature, what would it look like?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: let children predict which animal the mouse will meet next.
Third read: take turns being the mouse's voice for the repeated description.
books.lookFor: Look closely at the gruffalo's picture — can you spot all the features the mouse described before he appears?

books.title: Dear Zoo
books.author: Rod Campbell
books.why: A simple lift-the-flap structure that lets even the youngest children guess and join in before each reveal.
talkPrompts: Why do you think each animal gets sent back?
Which animal would you ask the zoo to send you, and why?
What do you think the zookeeper packs the animals in?
If the zoo sent you a surprise animal, what would you want it to be?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: cover the animal name and guess from the crate or box shape alone.
Third read: let children lift the flaps themselves and say the animal before you read the word.
books.lookFor: Look at the shape and size of each box or crate — does it give you a clue about what is inside before you look?

books.title: Each Peach Pear Plum
books.author: Janet and Allan Ahlberg
books.why: A rhyming 'I spy' structure that invites children to search the pictures for familiar storybook characters.
talkPrompts: Which storybook character did you spot first?
Why do you think the author chose to hide a different character on every page?
Which page's rhyme was your favourite, and why?
Can you think of your own two rhyming words to describe a picture?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: search for the hidden character together before turning each page.
Third read: let children say the rhyming word before you do.
books.lookFor: Each picture hides the character from the NEXT page somewhere in the scene — can you spot them hiding before they get their own page?

books.title: Owl Babies
books.author: Martin Waddell
books.why: A gentle, reassuring story about a worry — their mother owl being away — that resolves happily, told through three distinct characters.
talkPrompts: How do you think the three owl babies felt while their mother was away?
Which owl baby's reaction was most like how you'd feel?
Why do you think the mother owl went out at night?
What do the baby owls say to reassure each other?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: give each child one owl's repeated line to say.
Third read: notice how the pictures get darker and then lighter as the story moves through the night.
books.lookFor: Look at how close together the three owls are sitting on each page — does it change as the story goes on?

books.title: The Tiger Who Came to Tea
books.author: Judith Kerr
books.why: A warm, slightly wild 'what if' story about an enormous, unexpected visitor turning an ordinary tea time upside down.
talkPrompts: How do you think Sophie felt when the tiger first knocked on the door?
Why do you think the tiger ate and drank absolutely everything in the house?
What would you do if a tiger came to your house for tea?
Why do you think Daddy isn't cross when he hears what happened?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: count together everything the tiger eats and drinks.
Third read: act out how careful, or how enormous, each bite and sip should look.
books.lookFor: Look at how much smaller everything in the house looks compared to the tiger on each page.

books.title: Brown Bear, Brown Bear, What Do You See?
books.author: Bill Martin Jr
books.why: A simple, predictable question-and-answer pattern that's perfect for very young children to join in and anticipate.
talkPrompts: Can you remember which animal comes after the bird?
What colour is your favourite animal in the book?
If you were in the book, what would you be and what colour?
Why do you think every animal is looking at the one before it?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: let children say the animal's colour and name before you turn the page.
Third read: swap in a made-up animal and colour of your own at the end.
books.lookFor: Look closely at each animal's eyes — who are they looking at on every page?

books.title: Mr Gumpy's Outing
books.author: John Burningham
books.why: A patterned story where more and more characters ask to join a boat trip, each promising not to misbehave — then do anyway.
talkPrompts: Why do you think every animal makes the same kind of promise?
Which animal do you think caused the most trouble, and why?
What happened when the boat got too full?
Would you have let all those animals on board? Why or why not?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: predict what each new character will promise before you read it.
Third read: count how many characters are on the boat by the time it tips over.
books.lookFor: Count how many passengers are squeezed onto the boat right before it capsizes.

books.title: Room on the Broom
books.author: Julia Donaldson
books.why: A rhyming, repeated-refrain story about kindness and friendship, where sharing makes a tricky journey possible.
talkPrompts: Why do you think the witch keeps saying yes to each new animal?
What happens to the broom each time a new animal climbs on?
How do the animals help the witch at the end of the story?
What would you want to bring if you had room on the broom?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: let children predict which animal will ask to join next.
Third read: join in on the broomstick's repeated rhyme together.
books.lookFor: Look at how crowded the broomstick gets — can you count every animal riding on it at once?

books.title: Whatever Next!
books.author: Jill Murphy
books.why: An imaginative bedtime pretend-play story that turns everyday objects into a rocket and a moon adventure.
talkPrompts: What everyday things does Baby Bear use to make his rocket?
What do you think it would feel like to visit the moon?
Why do you think Baby Bear takes a picnic with him?
What would you build your own pretend rocket out of?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: spot each household object before it becomes part of the rocket.
Third read: act out getting dressed in Baby Bear's 'space suit' together.
books.lookFor: Look for the owl Baby Bear meets on the moon — what is the owl doing on each page it appears?

books.title: Handa's Surprise
books.author: Eileen Browne
books.why: A gentle guessing story set in a Kenyan village, with a repeated pattern and a lovely twist involving a mischievous goat.
talkPrompts: Which fruit do you think Akeyo will enjoy the most, and why?
What do you think keeps happening to the fruit in the basket?
Who do you think is really responsible for the surprise at the end?
Which fruit in the story have you never tried before?
rereadingIdeas: Second read: predict which animal will take the next fruit before you turn the page.
Third read: count how many different fruits go into the basket altogether.
books.lookFor: Look very closely at the background of each page — can you spot the goat following Handa all the way?
